recall_prompt: Say how you would count the chains from six different beads — why the circular count is halved, and the number.
insider_note: A chain is a circle that can also be turned over, so the count is (n − 1)!/2 and the division by 2 is the mark students lose — 120 is the round-table answer, not the chain answer.

steps.label: A chain is a circular arrangement that can be turned over
steps.margin_note: First mark. Beads on a chain form a circle, so (n − 1)! arrangements; and a chain can be turned over, so clockwise and anticlockwise are the same chain — halve it: (n − 1)!/2.
steps.memory_tip: A circle gives (n − 1)!, and a chain can be turned over, so halve it: (n − 1)!/2.

recall.must_convey: That beads on a chain are a circular arrangement, (n minus 1) factorial, halved because the chain can be turned over.
accept: circular arrangement is n minus one factorial and a chain can be flipped so divide by two
n minus one factorial by two because clockwise and anticlockwise are the same chain
a chain is a circle that can be turned over so half of n minus one factorial
circle ki n minus one factorial, chain ni flip cheyochu kabatti by two
the formula for chains is n minus one factorial over two

steps.why: On a circle, rotating an arrangement gives the same arrangement, which is why one bead is fixed and (n − 1)! counts the rest. A chain has no fixed side either, so each arrangement and its mirror image are one chain — hence the further division by 2.
common_mistakes: Using n! as for a row.
Using (n − 1)! without halving — that counts a ring that cannot be turned over, such as people at a round table.

steps.label: Evaluate for n = 6
steps.memory_tip: 5!/2 = 120/2 = 60. The 120 is the round-table answer, not the chain answer.

accept: five factorial by two is sixty
one twenty by two is sixty

steps.why: With n = 6, (n − 1)! = 120 and half of it is 60; the halving is what the question tests.
